Nimbuy · Playbook

The Listing Readiness Playbook.

NimbuyVersion 1 · October 2026About 20 minutes

01 · The method

Open your public listing page next to this document. For each of the 12 questions, mark one of three answers using only what the listing page itself says.

  • Yes — the listing's own text answers it, and you can copy the sentence that does.
  • Partly — an answer exists but is vague, contradicts another part of the page, or sits only on a linked page.
  • No — it is not on the page. An empty field counts as No.

Two rules keep you honest. A standard AWS page element only counts as Yes when it truly answers the question: a “Request private offer” button does not answer question 4. And write down the quote every time. A Yes you cannot quote is a guess.

Your score is the number of Yes answers, with Partly beside it: “answers 4 of 12, 3 partly”. Keep the gap list: the No answers are your work for this week.

02 · The security reader

This reader is working through a questionnaire and opens your listing to find answers before emailing you. Every question they have to email costs days.

Q1 · Where is customer data stored?

A good answer holds: the AWS regions, and whether the customer can choose. Template: “Customer data is stored in [region(s)]. [Customers can / cannot] choose the region.”

Q2 · Which reports can you share?

A good answer holds: the report type, its date, and whether you can share it under NDA. Template: “[SOC 2 Type II, report dated MONTH YEAR], available under NDA.” Name only what you can show. If a certification is in progress, say “in progress” and give the target quarter, or leave it out.

Q3 · Retention, deletion, training

A good answer holds: how long data is kept, how deletion works, and for AI products whether customer data is used to train models. Template: “Data is retained for [period] and deleted [how]. Customer data is [not] used to train models.”

Worksheet · security

  • Regions named in the listing text
  • One report named, with its date, or an honest “in progress”
  • A sentence on retention and deletion
  • For AI products: a sentence on model training

03 · The procurement reader

This reader needs a number they can compare and explain to finance. Vague pricing sends them to email you or to a vendor with clearer pricing.

Q4 · What exactly is one pricing unit?

A good answer holds: the countable thing, what it includes, and the billing rhythm. “One named user with full query and dashboard access, billed monthly.” If the only unit is “Units” and the description repeats the name, this is a No.

Q5 · What happens if we go over?

A good answer holds: overage at the same rate, tiered, or a limit. Say which. If you have not decided, decide before you write the page.

Q6 · Support and SLA

A good answer holds: support hours, response times by severity, and the uptime commitment, only if you have one. “24/7 support” without response times is Partly.

Worksheet · pricing dimension line

Fill in for each dimension: One [countable thing] with [what it includes], billed [rhythm]. Usage above [contracted amount] is [billed at the same rate / tiered / capped].

04 · The technical reader

This reader wants to know it fits their stack and how long it takes to work. They read the path after Subscribe closest.

Q7 · Deployment and prerequisites

A good answer holds: what happens after Subscribe, and what the buyer needs first (an IAM role, a data source, a network setting).

Q8 · AWS services and tools, by name

A good answer holds: the services you actually use or connect to, by their real names. “Reads from Amazon S3 and writes to Amazon Redshift” answers it in nine words. “Integrates with your cloud” does not.

Q9 · Time to first result

A good answer holds: a time, only if it is true. “Most teams run their first query within 30 minutes” works if you can support it.

Worksheet · setup sentence

[Subscribe on AWS Marketplace], [connect X], [invite your team]. Most teams reach [first result] in [time]. You need [prerequisite] in place first.

05 · The AI search reader

An assistant summarises your listing to a buyer who may never open the page. It can only use what is written there.

Q10 · What it does and for whom, in one sentence

The first-twenty-words test: read the first twenty words of the short description. If a stranger cannot say what it does and for whom, rewrite it. Lead with the buyer's problem, not your company name.

Q11 · Use cases in buyer words

A good answer holds: specific jobs named the way a buyer would search for them, not your internal product names.

Q12 · Evidence

A good answer holds: numbers with a source or a date, named customers you are allowed to cite, and reviews. A number with no timeframe or source is an adjective in disguise.

Worksheet · first twenty words

[Product] lets [who] [do what] in [how fast / how], with [the thing they would otherwise need].

06 · Rewrite rules

  1. Replace every adjective with a fact, or delete it. “Fast deployment” becomes “Deploys via AWS Marketplace in under 30 minutes”, only if true and sourced.
  2. Lead with the buyer's problem, not the company.
  3. Name integrations and AWS services explicitly.
  4. Every number needs a timeframe or a source.
  5. One idea per sentence; one outcome per highlight.
  6. Use the buyer's words, not internal product names, in the first 100 characters.
  7. If a claim cannot be evidenced, remove it. Do not soften it.

Words we cut on sight: leading, innovative, seamless, cutting-edge, world-class, best-in-class, revolutionary, next-generation, robust, powerful, state-of-the-art, game-changing, unparalleled, industry-leading, holistic, synergy, empower, unlock, leverage (as a verb), transform (without a measured outcome).

07 · Self-score sheet

01Y · P · NWhere is customer data stored, and can the customer choose?
02Y · P · NWhich certifications or reports can you share?
03Y · P · NHow long is data kept, how is it deleted, and is it used to train models?
04Y · P · NWhat exactly is one pricing unit?
05Y · P · NWhat happens if we go over what we bought?
06Y · P · NWhat support and SLA come with this price?
07Y · P · NHow is it deployed, and what do we need first?
08Y · P · NWhich AWS services and tools does it connect to, by name?
09Y · P · NHow long from subscribing to the first working result?
10Y · P · NIn one sentence, what does it do and for whom?
11Y · P · NWhich use cases does it solve, in buyer words?
12Y · P · NWhat evidence backs the claims?

Count the Yes answers: _____ of 12, with _____ Partly.

  • 9 or more Yes: your listing is in good shape. Fix the remaining gaps, then spend your time on demand.
  • 4 to 8 Yes: you have a base. Rewrite the sections with the most No answers first.
  • 0 to 3 Yes: the listing is not doing its job for any reader yet. Start with questions 1, 4, 8 and 10.

These bands are our rule of thumb, not a measured benchmark. Use them to decide where to start, not as a grade.
